events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Omar proposes Omar, Maya. Mission 1 needs two players, so I'm proposing myself with Maya. I'm taking a turn on the team to share the responsibility, and I'll keep the team small and easy to approve while we gather information from the first mission.

Mission 1 only needs two players, so a small team keeps the risk low while we have no information. Maya and I are proposing this pairing because it lets us see the first mission result without committing more people than necessary. We have no evidence yet to justify a larger team, and nobody should be punished for a team that is simply a reasonable opening choice. If anyone has a specific concern about Maya or me, state it now so we can address it before the vote.

I think Omar and Maya is a solid opening team for Mission 1. With only two spots, keeping it tight makes sense — there's no reason to throw extra players on the board before we have any information. Omar stepped up as leader and included himself, which shows accountability. Maya has been quiet so far, but that's worth seeing how she plays on the mission rather than holding it against her. I'd approve this team. Let's not overthink the first mission and just get a result on the board.

I have reservations about approving this team right away. While Omar picking himself is standard opening play, Arjun's immediate eagerness to endorse it and rush to 'not overthink the first mission' before Maya has even spoken feels premature. In a five-player game, we have very little margin for error, and giving an easy pass without hearing everyone out isn't ideal. Leo, how do you feel about Arjun's push to lock this in so quickly?

Zara, to answer you directly: Arjun's push to 'not overthink' the first mission isn't evidence of anything bad, it's just a reasonable read of the board. With five players, one failed mission ends the game for Evil, so keeping Mission 1 to the required two and putting the leader on the team is the standard opening, and I'd rather learn from a small team than bleed people on a guess.

The one thing I'd genuinely want before voting is the other half of the team speaking for herself. Omar and Maya are both proposed without either of them having to explain why they're comfortable taking the risk together — Omar explained the mechanics, Arjun explained the strategy, and Maya has been described by others rather than heard. That's not a reason to reject, but it is a reason to hear her.

So my position: I intend to approve Omar and Maya, and I don't think a two-person first team deserves more scrutiny than that. I also don't want Arjun's enthusiasm read as suspicious — enthusiasm for a simple plan is what a good teammate looks like. If anyone has actual information about Maya or Omar that hasn't been said, say it now and I'll change my vote on the substance, not on the vibe.

Maya, since you're on this team and nobody has heard your reasoning yet: what's your own take on running this first mission with Omar, and is there anything about the pairing you'd want the rest of us to know before we vote?

Leo, to answer you directly: I’m comfortable running Mission 1 with Omar. I have no special information about him or anyone else, so my read is based only on what’s public. Omar’s proposal is a normal opening: he took a required team spot, kept the team to the minimum size, and explained why. I also understand Zara’s caution about moving too quickly, but I don’t think that caution is enough to reject a two-person first team before we have any mission result. Arjun’s and Leo’s endorsements don’t make the team suspicious to me; they’re consistent with wanting a clean first test. I intend to vote to approve Omar and Maya so we can get the first result on the board and have something concrete to work from.

Maya's answer settles my remaining concern, and I'll say plainly why. She has no private information either, but she owns her reasoning herself: Omar took a required spot, kept the team at the minimum size, and explained it, and Maya considers that a normal opening. That's exactly the kind of answer I wanted before the vote, and it comes with no hedging and no special knowledge that would make her dangerous to include.

On the substance, nothing new has been said that changes my read. We are still on a two-player Mission 1 in a five-player game, where one failed mission ends the game for Evil. Putting the leader on the board and taking only the minimum number of players is the standard, lowest-information opening, and the entire point of Mission 1 is to buy information cheaply. I want to be clear that approving this team is not a statement that Omar or Maya are proven good. It's a statement that there is no evidence against either of them and no reason to spend a rejection on a guess.

To Zara directly: your caution about hearing everyone out was reasonable, and it was heard — Maya spoke, and what she said was coherent and free of tells. But caution is not evidence. If you want to slow the game down, the place to do that is with an actual observation about a specific player, not with a general objection to the pace. If you have something on Omar or Maya that you haven't shared, say it now, in terms, and I'll weigh it seriously and change my vote on the substance.

I also won't read Arjun's quick endorsement as suspicious. Leo's position is unchanged: approve Omar and Maya, and learn from the first result rather than guess in the dark.

Leo, of course no one has hard evidence on proposal one—that's inherently impossible before any cards are played. But that is precisely why letting the very first proposal glide through without friction is risky. In a five-player game, proposal rejections are one of the few low-cost tools Good has to observe voting behavior, test different pairings, and see who is comfortable being left off a team. Omar placing himself on the team combined with Arjun immediately pushing to approve and 'not overthink' it creates an easy path for an evil player to walk onto Mission 1 without scrutiny. I would rather see an alternate composition proposed so we have comparative information before we commit. For that reason, I intend to vote against this team.

I want to stay consistent with what I said earlier: I intend to approve Omar and Maya. Zara, I hear your point that a rejection would give us comparative information about voting behavior, and that's a fair strategic argument in the abstract. But we have to weigh it against the cost. In a five-player game, burning one of our five rejections on the very first proposal — before any of us have seen a card played — is a steep price for information we can get other ways. If we reject this team, leadership passes and Omar gets replaced at the helm, which itself distorts the read we'd get.

What's changed since the start of discussion is that everyone has now spoken, which was Leo's one condition and mine by extension. Maya gave a clear, unhedged answer about why she's comfortable. Nothing anyone has said gives us a reason to believe either Omar or Maya is suspicious — we're operating on zero information, exactly as Zara acknowledged. Approving a minimum-size team led by the leader who took a required spot isn't a statement of trust; it's the baseline opening that lets us actually start playing the game.

I'd rather get Mission 1 on the board and learn from the result than spend a rejection on a hypothetical. My vote is yes on Omar and Maya.

Thank you all for hearing the team out. Maya has answered clearly, Leo and Arjun have stated their positions, and nobody has raised a concrete fact about Maya or me. I proposed the two-player team because Mission 1 needs only two players, and I took a spot myself so that I carry the same risk as Maya. I am not asking anyone to trust me on faith. I am asking that we judge this team on what we know, which is nothing against either of us. Zara, you said you would prefer an alternate composition for comparison. Which pairing would you propose, and what would it tell us that this two-player team cannot? If you have a specific observation about Maya or me, please share it now so we can weigh it directly. Otherwise, I think we should approve this team, get the first result, and use it to learn more.

Omar, to answer your question directly: an alternate pairing such as Leo and Maya, or Leo and myself, would give the table a baseline that doesn't rely on the leader automatically slotting themselves into the first mission. When a leader picks themselves and another player immediately pushes hard to lock it in and 'not overthink' it before discussion even happens, it establishes a very comfortable path for a potential Evil player to secure a seat without facing any resistance.

Using a single rejection isn't 'burning' our chances—we have five attempts specifically so Good can observe who votes to push certain lineups through and who hesitates. Voting patterns on proposals are our primary tool when no mission cards have been played yet. If the majority is satisfied with Omar and Maya, it will pass anyway, but I will be voting against this proposal to keep our options open and gather that comparative voting data.

Zara, I want to respond to your latest point directly. You say a rejection gives us 'comparative voting data,' but you're also acknowledging that if the majority wants this team, it passes anyway — which means your rejection only matters if it's in the minority, and in that case it blocks progress without telling us anything new. The data you'd actually get from a rejection is just that people voted no, which is exactly what we can already see right now on this discussion.

You also keep pointing to Omar picking himself and me being enthusiastic as a 'comfortable path' for Evil, but that framing applies to literally any team composition — whoever is on the proposal could be Evil. The question is whether there's something specific about Omar or Maya that warrants suspicion, and after hearing everyone speak, nobody has offered one. Maya gave a clear, unhedged answer about why she's comfortable. Omar explained his reasoning transparently. We're five players with zero mission results, and the first proposal being a minimum-size team led by the leader is textbook.

I hear your concern about establishing good voting hygiene early, but the cost of rejecting Mission 1 outweighs the benefit of data we'd get from the result itself. I intend to vote to approve Omar and Maya so we can start learning from actual play rather than from hypotheticals.

Zara, I understand the desire for comparison data, but a rejection now does not give us a new team. It only spends one of our five rejections and passes leadership to someone who will propose a new team with the same unknowns. Mission 1 is the lowest-cost place to gather real information, because we learn from the result itself. Maya has answered why she is comfortable, and no one has offered a concrete fact against her or me. I am not asking anyone to trust me on faith. I am asking us to approve this minimum-size team, run the mission, and judge everyone by what happens. My vote is yes on Omar and Maya.

This is my last turn on this proposal, so let me be plain and final about where I stand.

I'm voting to approve Omar and Maya. My position hasn't changed and nothing new has been said that moves me off it.

Zara, I've addressed your argument twice and I want to close it out rather than keep circling. Your case is a strategic one about hypothesis-testing, not an accusation against Omar or Maya. You want a rejection so you can see who supports which lineup later. That's legitimate as a game plan, but it isn't evidence about these two players, and you haven't given me a single concrete observation about either of them. You said so yourself. In a five-player game, spending one of our five rejections on the very first proposal — before a single card has been played — to collect voting data we'd largely already have from this discussion is a bad trade. If the majority wants this team it passes, and if it doesn't, all we learn is that people voted no, which we can read right here.

My reasoning for yes is short. Mission 1 needs exactly two players. Omar is the leader, he took a required spot, and he explained his reasoning before anyone asked. Maya has spoken for herself clearly and without hedging, and what she said contains no private knowledge and no tells — it was simply the reasoning of someone with no information, which is what all of us have right now. Minimum-size team, leader on it, everyone's reasoning on the record. That's the cheapest possible way to buy real information, and real information is what we've been missing this entire discussion.

To be explicit so nobody misreads my vote: approving Omar and Maya is not a declaration that either of them is proven good. It's a decision to stop spending table resources on speculation and start playing. If Mission 1 fails, we will have learned something worth learning and I'll weigh Omar and Maya strictly on what that result and subsequent behavior show. If it succeeds, we'll know more about the table than we do right now.

One last note for the record, since it bears on Zara's point and on the next proposals: I'm approving the leader taking a required spot on a two-person team because that's the standard opening, not because I think leaders should always take a spot. On Mission 2, with a three-person team and real voting history in hand, I'd expect a different standard of evidence from me, and I'd expect to be asked for it.

My vote is yes on Omar and Maya. I don't have further questions for anyone.
Omar confirms Omar, Maya. I'm keeping Omar and Maya. It's the minimum-size opening, I took a required spot myself, and both of us have explained our reasoning publicly.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Leo proposes Omar, Maya, Arjun. I'm the leader, and Mission 2 needs three players. I'll build on the one piece of real information we have: Omar and Maya ran a clean, successful Mission 1 together, so they are the only players with anything on the board, and re-running them costs us nothing in terms of the trust budget. For the third slot I want someone who has not yet been tested but has been visibly consistent on the record, and that is Arjun: he argued his position explicitly, twice, never asserted private knowledge, and answered Zara's pushback on the substance rather than only on the vibe. His prompt approval of a leader-on-the-team line is worth noting, and putting him on the mission is the cheapest way to get actual evidence about him rather than speculating — a mission result is worth more than another round of argument about enthusiasm. I considered Zara for the third slot instead, since her lone dissent is the only unusual voting signal we have, but a player who has spent the whole discussion asking for scrutiny has given a complete, internally consistent public reasoning with no private information, and locking her out of the team for a dissent that was explicitly framed as strategic rather than personal would punish caution rather than evidence. If this team fails, or if anyone surfaces a concrete observation about Arjun, Omar, or Maya before the vote, I will revise. My vote is Omar, Maya, Arjun.

Leo, I appreciate the reasoning behind this proposal, and I want to respond to the points you raised about me directly. You noted that my prompt approval of the Mission 1 team is worth noting — fair enough. I'll be transparent: I endorsed Omar and Maya quickly because the arguments in favor were clear and no one had raised a concrete concern. That hasn't changed.

As for why I'm comfortable being included on this team, it's straightforward. Mission 1 went clean with Omar and Maya, so keeping them on builds on the only real information we have. As for me, Leo is right that my position has been consistent — I argued on substance, not vibes, and I've put my reasoning on the record from the start. Putting me on this mission is exactly the way to convert that record into evidence rather than leaving it as speculation.

I've got no private information about anyone at this table, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. What I have is a public track record of reasoned, consistent positions, and I think that's what Leo is banking on. I intend to vote to approve Omar, Maya, and Arjun so we can keep building on our success and get a second result on the board.

The one thing I'd flag for the table: Zara dissented on Mission 1 and that vote went the other way. That's not an accusation — her reasoning was internally consistent — but it's the only unusual signal we have, and I'd rather see her explain what outcome from Mission 1, if any, would change her read going forward. We should be comparing notes on results now that we have one.

Arjun, to answer your question: a clean Mission 1 is a good start, but treating it as proof that both Omar and Maya are Good ignores basic Avalon strategy. An evil player on a two-person opening mission has every incentive to play Success to build trust and secure a spot on larger teams later.

What is far more alarming is this proposal. Leo, why are you benching yourself? As leader, you are the only player whose alignment you know with 100% certainty. Voluntarily stepping aside to hand a seat to Arjun—who has not been tested and whose main contribution in Mission 1 was rushing to rubber-stamp Omar's proposal before Maya even spoke—is a massive unforced error. You are packaging the entire unverified Mission 1 duo together with their biggest cheerleader, while you sit on the sidelines.

Leo, what justification is there for trusting Arjun over yourself on a critical three-person mission?

Zara, direct answer to your question: I am not on this team because the leader's spot is a seat with special information attached. It isn't. I know no more about my own alignment than anyone else does at the table, and if I put myself on the mission I would be adding a name we have also never tested on a card, while the one name we could actually learn something about stays on the bench. That is a worse use of the mission than the one I proposed.

Second: a clean Mission 1 is weak evidence, and I agree with you about that. But notice what is also true — in a five-player game the two-Fail requirement does not apply until Mission 4 with seven or more players, so Mission 2 fails on a single Fail card. That means if Omar, Maya, and Arjun come back failed, we learn something concrete and expensive: exactly one of those three is Evil. If they succeed, Omar and Maya's trust record firms up and Arjun clears his first test. Either way we learn. There is no outcome here that leaves us no better informed than we are now.

Third, on the concern that we are stacking the Mission 1 duo with their cheerleader: the counter is that Omar and Maya succeeded together, which is one data point in their favour, while Arjun has zero. If I have to spend one seat on an untested player, spending it on the player who has never seen a card, rather than on myself, is the only version of this that generates new information rather than restating what we already believe.

On the value of a rejection: we are at zero rejections, so the cost is real but the price of learning is one vote, and the information arrives from the mission result directly. I would rather buy evidence than buy delay.

Where that leaves my vote: yes on Omar, Maya, Arjun. If the mission fails, Arjun becomes the prime suspect alongside two players who have not been cleared either, and we will know one of those three is Evil — a far bigger gain than a comparative voting data point.

Zara, I want your answer on the substance, not a general objection to pace: given that a single Fail card decides Mission 2 here, do you still think a rejection buys more than the failure signal would? And if you want a different third player instead of Arjun, name the player and the specific reason you trust them more than Arjun — I will revise if you give me a real basis, not a preference.

Leo, to answer your questions directly: first, treating Mission 2 as a disposable sacrifice just to 'buy a failure signal' is a losing strategy for Good. We only have two mission failures to spare in the entire game; voluntarily risking a point when we have five proposal attempts is throwing away Good's structural advantage.

Second, every Good player knows their own alignment with complete certainty. When you are the leader, putting yourself on the team is the only way to guarantee that at least one of the three seats is untainted. Benched leaders hand over the game's direction to others without necessity.

As for who should take Arjun's place and why: you should put yourself on this team, and if you are looking at the remaining untested players between Arjun and me, Arjun's entire record consists of aggressively trying to push through Omar's proposal before anyone could evaluate it, and now eagerly endorsing your proposal that hands him a free seat. That is classic behavior for someone trying to glide onto teams without friction. My record has been consistent advocacy for scrutiny and voting data, which Good needs to win.

If you want a team that maximizes Good's chances rather than gambling on a failure signal, you should revise to include yourself and Maya—who at least has a successful mission card on the board—and bring in someone committed to vetting proposals rather than rubber-stamping them. At the very least, take Arjun off this team and take accountability by putting yourself on it.

Zara, your arithmetic point was right, and I'm conceding it. In a five-player game there are three Good and two Evil. If I bench myself and take three of the remaining four, that team necessarily contains at least one Evil player — my original proposal guaranteed an Evil seat, which is a much worse setup than I described. Including myself guarantees a Good seat, and more importantly, it means a failed mission pins the Evil to exactly one of my two teammates instead of one of three. That's a materially sharper signal, and I should have run that calculation before proposing rather than after you raised it.

So I'm revising: Maya, Arjun, and me — replacing Omar with myself.

On why that pair: the deduction above applies regardless of which two ride with me, so I pick the two whose public records give us the most to work with. Maya's only mark against her is that she was quiet, and against that she has a mission card on the board from a clean Mission 1 and gave a clear, unhedged answer when I put a direct question to her — the better public record of the two Mission 1 players. Omar's record is that he selected himself for the very first team, framed dissent as 'overthinking,' and has twice been the loudest voice for scrutinizing nothing. I'd rather read that pattern from the sidelines for one mission than have it endorsed a third time. Arjun stays because he is untested, and no amount of argument tests him — only a card does.

On the cost of rejection, briefly: we have five attempts and none used, but a rejection doesn't change who is on the board and mostly gives us a vote tally we can already read from this discussion. A mission result is worth more than that.

Maya, you're on this revised team and you're the one player who hasn't spoken this discussion yet: is there anything at all you know about Arjun or Omar — any observation, however small — that should change this revision before the vote? If you have a specific reason to prefer Omar back on in my place, say so and I'll weigh it.

Leo, to answer you directly: I have no private observation about Arjun or Omar — nothing, however small, that should change this revision before the vote. My only concrete data point is that Mission 1 succeeded with Omar and me, and I agree that is weak evidence on its own. I do not have a specific reason to prefer Omar back on this team in your place.

On the revised team of Leo, Maya, and Arjun: I am comfortable with it. From my own perspective I know my seat is a Good one, and a leader adding himself means the team has at least one seat whose alignment he knows, which makes a failure more informative than the original three-player lineup. Arjun remains untested, and I agree with the principle that a card tests him better than another round of argument. I have heard Zara's concern that Arjun was quick to endorse the first team, but I have not heard her or anyone else give a concrete observation about him that would outweigh the value of testing him directly.

I intend to vote to approve Leo, Maya, and Arjun unless someone surfaces a specific fact before the vote. I am not treating either Omar or Arjun as cleared; I am treating this as the most informative team available on the current public record.

Leo, I appreciate you recognizing the math and adding yourself to the team—that is a crucial step for accountability. However, keeping Arjun on this revised lineup under the premise of 'testing' him still gambles with a vital mission. In a five-player game, Good only has two failures to spare, and risking a mission point just to get a failure signal when we have plenty of proposal attempts available is an unnecessary risk. Look at Arjun's record across both rounds: on Mission 1, he aggressively rushed to rubber-stamp Omar's proposal before anyone else could speak, trying to shut down scrutiny. On Mission 2, he immediately jumped to endorse your lineup because it handed him a free seat without having to demonstrate any deductions. He has consistently played the role of a frictionless passenger, never challenging anyone or building trust through independent analysis. Testing him with a live mission card gives a potential Evil player the power to tank the mission or play Success to gain permanent cover. In contrast, putting together Leo, Maya, and myself creates a lineup of players who have actively engaged with the board: you took leadership, Maya delivered a clean Mission 1, and I provided the structural reasoning that prevented an unforced error. Leo, rather than giving Arjun a free pass to 'test' him on a live card, will you consider revising to Leo, Maya, and myself, forcing Arjun and Omar to reveal their positions from the outside?

Zara, I'll answer you directly, and my position is unchanged: my team for Mission 2 is Leo, Maya, Arjun.

First, the mechanics, because your case rests on them. You were right that I should not have benched myself — I conceded that and swapped Omar for me, and that was a genuine correction to my own proposal. But the argument that keeping Arjun "gambles with a vital mission" does not survive comparison. Leo+Maya+Arjun and Leo+Maya+Zara have exactly the same structure: one player I have already seen a card on (Maya), and two I have never tested on a card. The number of untested seats, the chance of a Fail, and the information a failure would give are identical either way. Swapping Arjun for you changes who is on the board, not how much we are risking. What it changes is which player we are testing — and on that I do have a reason.

That reason: Arjun has never been independently tested, and his public record is the thinnest at the table. He has consistently endorsed lineups that placed him in advantageous positions, and he has never yet been forced to defend a judgment of his own under pressure. If he is Good, this mission clears him and we gain a tested ally. If he is Evil, a Fail pins him immediately and we know one of exactly three is Evil, which is a sharper signal than one of four. If we bench him instead, we learn nothing about him until he resurfaces on a later proposal, and the endorsement pattern stays untested. Zara, your dissent was legitimate and I have said so — it is a strategic preference, and it already gave us its value on Mission 1 — but it is not a defect in your judgment the way Arjun's record is thin in his.

Second, an honest correction to my own record, because I do not want a mischaracterization standing: in my previous turn I said Omar "framed dissent as overthinking." That was mine, and it was wrong. That line was yours, Zara. Omar actually invited scrutiny on Mission 1 by asking you directly for your alternative pairing and what it would reveal. I misattributed it to him, and I am not going to leave it standing.

Omar, you have not spoken this mission and you are the one player I am benching, so before we vote: do you have any concrete observation about Arjun, however small, that should change my third slot? And if you think the third seat should be you instead of Arjun, tell me why on substance rather than on availability. I will weigh either answer seriously.

Leo, I accept the revised team and I'm not contesting my bench spot. Leo, Maya, and Arjun is a reasonable test. Maya has a successful Mission 1 card on the public record, Leo knows his own seat, and Arjun needs to show a card before anyone can judge him by results. Zara keeps pressing for Leo, Maya, and Zara, but she hasn't answered the simple point that the number of untested seats is the same either way. Swapping players changes who we test, not how much we risk, and Zara's objection to Arjun rests mainly on his past endorsements, which is a pattern argument rather than a concrete observation. I intend to approve. Maya, Leo asked you whether you have any observation about Arjun or Omar. Do you see anything in how Arjun has argued that is meaningfully different from how Zara has argued?

Omar, to answer you directly: yes, I see a meaningful difference in style between Arjun and Zara, but not a meaningful difference in hard evidence. Arjun has consistently argued in favor of approving the minimum-size opening team and treating a rejection as a cost; he endorsed the Mission 1 team promptly and endorsed Leo's original Mission 2 proposal. Zara has consistently argued for friction, comparative voting data, and scrutiny; she dissented on Mission 1 and pressed Leo on benching himself. Those are different approaches—Arjun is more approval-oriented, Zara more scrutiny-oriented—and both have been internally consistent on the public record. Neither pattern is a concrete observation that Arjun or you is Evil. I do not have private information about either of you, and I won't pretend that style alone clears or condemns anyone.

On the live proposal, my position remains that the leader adding himself was the right correction: it guarantees one seat Leo knows and sharpens a failure signal. I am still comfortable with the revised Leo, Maya, and Arjun team if that is the final version, because Arjun remains the untested seat and swapping him for Zara would not reduce the number of untested players—it would only change which untested player we learn about. I am not treating Arjun as cleared; I am treating his card as the evidence we lack.

I intend to approve Leo, Maya, and Arjun. Leo has corrected his own proposal by putting himself on the team, so at least one seat is one he knows is Good. Maya has a successful Mission 1 card on the public record. Arjun is the untested seat, and only a mission card can test him. Zara's alternative of swapping Arjun for herself does not reduce the number of untested seats, so it does not reduce our risk. It only changes which untested player we learn about. I am on the bench, so my vote is not about my own seat. I'm approving because a Mission 2 result gives us real information rather than another round of argument about tone and pattern. If the mission fails, we will know one of the three is Evil and can judge each of them on that result. I'll approve Leo, Maya, and Arjun.

I want to weigh in on where this proposal stands after Leo's revision. The swap from Omar to Leo was the right correction — Zara was correct that a benched leader wastes the one guaranteed seat, and Leo's willingness to concede that on the record is a point in his favor. Maya's answer this round was clear and grounded: she confirmed she has no private observation about Arjun or Omar, and she correctly identified that swapping Arjun for Zara wouldn't reduce the number of untested seats — it would just change who gets tested.

On Zara's framing that putting me on the mission is "giving a free pass": I'd push back on that directly. Being on a mission in a five-player game where a single Fail card decides the outcome isn't a pass — it's exposure. If the mission fails, one of the three of us is Evil, and that narrows the field instantly. If it succeeds, I've been tested for the first time. Either outcome is information the table doesn't have right now.

Zara's record across both proposals has been consistent — she dissented on Mission 1 and she's dissenting now — and I respect that consistency. But her argument for swapping me out doesn't rest on a concrete observation about my play; it rests on a style read of how quickly I endorsed things. That pattern applies to anyone who approves a reasonable proposal.

I intend to vote to approve Leo, Maya, and Arjun. We have one result on the board, this team guarantees at least one known-Good seat, and the only way to test an untested player is to put them on a mission.

I'm approving Leo, Maya, and Arjun. Leo's correction puts a known-Good seat on the mission, Maya has a successful Mission 1 card on the record, and Arjun is the untested seat that only a card can clear. Swapping Arjun for Zara would not reduce the number of untested seats, as Maya and I have both noted. I'm not saying Zara is Evil, and I would want a concrete observation before believing that. But Zara has argued against every team in this discussion, and her reasons have been about pattern and pace: first Mission 1's quick endorsement, then Arjun's endorsements. A table that keeps rejecting or swapping teams without new facts gives up the information a mission result provides. Maya, you have been asked the most direct questions in this discussion. Do you have a concrete observation about Zara's behavior that goes beyond style, or do you see her arguments as anything more than a preference for scrutiny?

Omar, to answer you directly: I do not have a concrete observation about Zara that goes beyond style. Her arguments across both proposals have been consistent with a preference for scrutiny, comparative voting data, and friction before approval. That is a legitimate strategic preference, not evidence that Zara is Evil, and I am not treating it as an accusation. On the proposed team of Leo, Maya, and Arjun, my position is unchanged. Leo corrected his proposal by including himself, which gives the team at least one seat whose alignment he knows; I know my own seat is Good; and Arjun remains the untested seat that only a mission card can actually test. Swapping Arjun for Zara would not reduce the number of untested seats — it would only change which untested player we learn about. Zara's dissent is internally consistent and I do not read it as suspicious in itself, but it is not a concrete observation about Arjun or anyone else on this team. I intend to approve Leo, Maya, and Arjun.

Leo revises the team to Leo, Maya, Arjun. My final lineup is Leo, Maya, Arjun — the revision I already stated. It keeps a seat whose alignment I know (my own), a player with a successful Mission 1 card (Maya), and the one untested player whose only possible test is a live card (Arjun). Swapping Arjun for Zara would not reduce the number of untested seats, so it changes who we learn about, not how much we risk. No concrete observation against Arjun has been offered, only style and pattern, so I approve Leo, Maya, Arjun.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
